segments.title: Opening: The Fog and the Machine

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close, unhurried look at one of the greatest novels in the English language.
Charles Dickens published Bleak House in monthly parts between 1852 and 1853, and it has never quite let readers go.
It is at once a savage satire of the legal system, a gothic mystery, a love story, and — many would argue — the finest sustained piece of prose fiction in English.
In this opening segment, we are beginning where the novel itself begins — with atmosphere, with fog, with dread, and with the long shadow of Chesney Wold.
Three brilliant readers have joined me today, and I want to introduce each of them properly.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who thinks about the architecture of fiction the way a great conductor thinks about a score — every structural choice is audible to her.

Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has voiced more classic novels on audio than almost anyone alive — he hears Dickens the way Dickens heard himself, in the voice, in the room, in performance.

And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since adolescence — she brings the reader's intimacy, the re-reader's eye, the person who stops mid-paragraph because a sentence has done something astonishing.
We begin with the ghost — with the crippled lady of the Ghost's Walk, and with the extraordinary scene at Chesney Wold that sets the curse in motion.
The thing you have to understand about Dickens — and about this novel in particular — is that he builds dread the way a great composer builds toward a climax.
The Ghost's Walk sequence is one of the most extraordinary pieces of gothic writing in Victorian fiction — and it arrives almost before you've settled in.
We're given this woman — the crippled ancestral lady — who never complains, never speaks of her pain, and simply, day after day, forces herself up and down that terrace.
Dickens gives us this extraordinary phrase: she went "up and down, up and down, up and down" — that triple repetition is relentless, it is the rhythm of her suffering.
"up and down, up and down, up and down, in sun and shadow, with greater difficulty every day."
That "in sun and shadow" — four words — carries the whole passage of time, years of endurance, and the indifference of the world.
And then she drops — and the curse she pronounces is one of the finest speeches in the novel.

"I will die here where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen for my step!"
She is still there, hauntingly, every time Lady Dedlock paces that walk in the present-day narrative.
What strikes me technically about that curse is the anaphora — "I will walk here" repeated three times — but it's not decorative.
It's structural prophecy — Dickens is laying in a formal promise to the reader, and the entire Chesney Wold subplot is the fulfilment of that promise.
And notice how the novel earns this moment — we are told she "never spoke to any one" of her pain, which means when she does speak, it has enormous weight.
Her silence throughout her suffering makes the curse erupt with that much more force — Dickens has been storing up the pressure for this one release.
And it pays off later — in the present narrative — when Esther herself sits near the Ghost's Walk and glimpses Lady Dedlock approaching through the wood.
That scene — when Esther sees Lady Dedlock emerging through the wood — is one I return to again and again.
Because Esther has just been picturing the ghost — the female shape haunting the walk — and then an actual woman begins to emerge from the trees.
Dickens handles the slow reveal with extraordinary care. The figure resolves by degrees.
"By little and little it revealed itself to be a woman's — a lady's — Lady Dedlock's."
Those em dashes — "a woman's — a lady's — Lady Dedlock's" — are doing something remarkable.
Each dash is a beat of recognition, and recognition here is terrifying, because Esther is, though she doesn't yet know it fully, recognising her mother.
The ghost of the ancestral woman and the living woman at the centre of the secret collapse into the same moment.
Caroline has touched on something that I think is the beating heart of what Dickens is doing with setting in this novel — haunting is not metaphor, it is mechanism.
The past is not atmospheric wallpaper — it literally, materially walks up to you through the trees.
And what I love about the passage is that small, grounding detail — Charley gathering violets nearby while all this gothic machinery is being set in motion.
That contrast — violets and doom — is absolutely Dickens at his most controlled.
And the urgency — when the machinery finally runs at full speed — Dickens delivers it through Bucket, and it is quite something.
There is a scene where Bucket addresses Jarndyce — appealing to him to let Esther accompany the search for Lady Dedlock — and the rhetoric is extraordinary.
Bucket builds the case, layer by layer — the lost hours, the danger of desperation, the hold that Esther's presence could give him — and then delivers this:
"If I follow her alone, she, being in ignorance of what Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, has communicated to me, may be driven to desperation.

But if I follow her in company with a young lady, answering to the description of a young lady that she has a tenderness for — I ask no question, and I say no more than that — she will give me credit for being friendly."
"I ask no question, and I say no more than that" — Bucket knows everything and chooses to name nothing.
That tact is the measure of his intelligence — and his decency.
The haunted house, the detective, the secret mother — all of it converging.

In our next segment, we'll look more closely at the novel's two narrators — Esther's intimate voice and the omniscient present-tense voice — and what Dickens gains from keeping them in such careful tension.

segments.title: The Architecture of Entanglement: Dickens's Narrative Web

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the series where we take one of the greatest novels in the English language apart — carefully — to see how it works.

I'm your host, and today we're looking at something central to Bleak House: the way Dickens builds a narrative web so intricate that characters, objects, and fates become mysteriously, fatally entangled.
With me today are three voices I'm genuinely delighted to have around this table.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley teaches creative writing and thinks about how novels are built — the architecture, the craft decisions, the single image that carries a whole chapter's weight.
Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more classic novels than perhaps anyone alive, and approaches Dickens first as a performer — he hears the prose the way a conductor hears a score.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has been returning to it ever since — she brings the reader's eye, and a fierce loyalty to the characters.
Eleanor, let's begin with you — because the passage I want to start with is one of those moments where Dickens plants a small object and watches it travel across the whole novel.
Yes — and this is one of the things that makes Bleak House structurally unlike almost anything else in the Victorian novel.
A handkerchief — a simple domestic object — becomes a carrier of fate.
Esther places it over a dead baby in a brickmaker's cottage, and in that moment she doesn't yet know what she is setting in motion.
And Dickens gives us Esther's retrospective voice, which is crucial — she is narrating from a point of knowledge she didn't have when she lived through the event.
So she can write, and this is the passage I keep coming back to —

"How little I thought, when I raised my handkerchief to look upon the tiny sleeper underneath and seemed to see a halo shine around the child through Ada's drooping hair as her pity bent her head — how little I thought in whose unquiet bosom that handkerchief would come to lie after covering the motionless and peaceful breast!"
That doubled phrase — "how little I thought" — enacts the very shape of irony that the whole novel runs on.
We are reading backwards and forwards at once — tenderness and dread occupying the same sentence.
What undoes me about that passage every time is the word "unquiet."
The baby is "motionless and peaceful" — death as stillness — but the bosom that will eventually hold that handkerchief is "unquiet."
Dickens has compressed an entire moral and emotional contrast into two adjectives separated by dozens of chapters.
And the halo around the child, seen through Ada's hair — that image of innocence and pity together — it makes what comes after all the more devastating.
Reading that passage aloud, you feel immediately why Dickens dictated so much of his prose — it's built for breath.
That long suspended first clause — "how little I thought, when I raised my handkerchief" — it holds you in suspense before dropping you into the revelation.
As a performer, you have to resist the temptation to signal the grief too early — the sentence does it for you, if you trust it.
And then there's the ending of the scene — Esther and Ada leave the woman standing at the door, calling "Jenny, Jenny!" in her "old soothing manner."
That detail — the voice repeating a name into absence — is pure Dickens at his most theatrical and most genuinely sad.
And what's remarkable is how the web of entanglement in this novel isn't just thematic — it's structural, distributed across two entirely different narrative voices.
Esther's first-person retrospective and the omniscient third-person narrator don't just alternate — they triangulate.
Each voice knows things the other doesn't — or withholds things the other reveals.
That double-vision is how Dickens keeps the reader in a state of perpetual partial knowledge — which is, of course, exactly the condition the novel diagnoses in its portrait of Chancery.
That connection between the novel's form and its subject is something I want to press on — and Richard Carstone is perhaps the character who most fully embodies what Chancery does to a person.
Eleanor, you've been looking closely at Richard — and there's a passage in Chapter Twenty-Three where he tries to articulate something about his own character with painful self-awareness.
Richard is one of the great tragic figures in Victorian fiction, and what makes him tragic rather than merely pathetic is precisely this self-knowledge that can't save him.
He knows what he is.
He says to Esther, with his characteristic blend of frankness and sorrow —

"I understand you, and I wish to heaven I were a more constant sort of fellow... If I were a more constant sort of fellow, I should have held on either to Badger or to Kenge and Carboy like grim death, and should have begun to be steady and systematic by this time, and shouldn't be in debt, and —"
And then the sentence just — breaks off.

That trailing dash is one of the most carefully placed punctuation marks in the novel — Richard literally cannot complete the thought because completing it would mean accepting a future he can't yet see.
What I find heartbreaking is the parenthetical — "I don't mean constant to Ada, for I love her dearly — better and better every day."
He rushes to protect Ada from any implication that he is inconstant in love — which of course he isn't.
His tragedy is that his devotion to Ada and his devotion to the suit become entangled — indistinguishable, finally, in his own mind.
Dickens also gives him that wonderful moment of self-aware helplessness: "Somehow, I mean something that I can't very well express, but you'll make it out."
He's appealing to Esther to understand what he can't articulate — and of course she does, because she always does, and that's almost unbearable.
Playing Richard — and I have voiced him in audio — is an exercise in calibrating decline without ever playing the decline directly.
Every time you think you've found his bottom note, Dickens pulls the floor away again.
But here, in this conversation with Esther, there's still a kind of music to him — that earnest "frankest and most feeling manner" Dickens specifies.
He's not yet hollowed out.
Which makes what Vholes does to him all the more monstrous — and Vholes, as a comic creation, is absolutely diabolical.

Since you've raised Vholes — let's go there, because Eleanor has been looking at the extraordinary moment in Chapter Sixty where Vholes delivers what amounts to a professional death sentence on Richard.
Vholes is Dickens's great satirical portrait of the law as a living organism that feeds on its clients — and the prose of his speeches enacts the very quality it describes.
It's inward, dispassionate, procedural — and devastating.
He tells Esther, hiding the catastrophe inside a recitation of professional duty —
"I HAVE carried it out; I do carry it out. But I will not smooth things over to any connexion of Mr. C.'s on any account."
And then, without pause, he pronounces: Richard's affairs are in a very bad way, Richard himself is in a very bad way, and the marriage was exceedingly ill-advised.
Three hammer-blows, each delivered in the same flat register, and then he immediately pivots to cheerfully greeting Richard when he walks in.
The tonal whiplash is the joke — and the horror.
That pivot to "Am I here, sir? Yes, I thank you; I am here, Mr. C." — I defy anyone to read that without an involuntary laugh followed immediately by a chill.
Vholes notes in his diary, for the record, that he used the words "openly carried on."
The diary detail is perfect — the man preserves the form of transparency to ensure no actual transparency ever occurs.
He is, in the purest sense, a creature of process — and process, in this novel, is what kills.
And yet Tulkinghorn operates by exactly the same logic — process as weapon, duty as disguise.
The passage Eleanor has been looking at in Chapter Forty-One — Tulkinghorn laying out his case to Lady Dedlock — reads almost like Vholes's dark twin.
He argues, in that Dickensian phrase, in his "jog-trot style" —
"If I inflicted this shock upon him to-morrow morning, how could the immediate change in him be accounted for? What could have caused it?"
He invokes Sir Leicester's health not out of care for him — but as a constraint on Lady Dedlock's freedom.
"You are to remember that it would not affect you merely — whom I cannot at all consider in this business — but your husband, Lady Dedlock, your husband."
That parenthetical — "whom I cannot at all consider" — is as cold a thing as Dickens ever wrote.
And notice how the repetition of "your husband, Lady Dedlock, your husband" works as a kind of incantation — it's not information, it's pressure.
Tulkinghorn is using the most intimate possible form of address to enact the most ruthless possible form of control.
And this is where Dickens's architecture reveals itself: the entanglement isn't just plot — it's the way power works through language.
I want to bring us to Ada — because set against all this legal machinery, Ada and her love for Richard represent something Dickens clearly holds very dear.
Eleanor, you've been looking at two passages that show Ada in the full arc of devotion — Chapter Fifty-One and Chapter Sixty.
The Chapter Fifty-One passage is one of the most painterly moments in the novel — Ada's gesture is so precisely choreographed that you can see it.
Listen to the sequence of actions Dickens gives us —
"my darling rose, put off her bonnet, kneeled down beside him with her golden hair falling like sunlight on his head, clasped her two arms round his neck, and turned her face to me."
Five verbs in succession: rose, put off, kneeled, clasped, turned.
Each one is a distinct act of devotion — and the rhythm accelerates until it lands on "turned her face to me."
Esther sees everything — and by turning to Esther, Ada makes Esther a witness to a love that transcends what language can quite hold.
That image — golden hair falling like sunlight on his head — is a kind of benediction.
It echoes the halo around the baby in Chapter Eight — Ada's hair framing innocence, framing the dying.
And then in Chapter Sixty, Ada speaks her extraordinary vision of redemption through the child she's carrying.
She looks forward "through years and years" to a future where a son — Richard's son — walks in sunshine with him, saying —
"I thank God this is my father! Ruined by a fatal inheritance, and restored through me!"
"Fatal inheritance" — there it is.
Jarndyce and Jarndyce is the true inheritance, and Ada knows it — and she imagines a redemption precisely through the next generation escaping what destroyed this one.
What's remarkable is how Dickens balances Ada's speech on the edge between hope and elegy.
She speaks of when she will be "growing old, or when I am dead perhaps" — she includes her own death in the vision with an almost serene matter-of-factness.
The hope is real, the love is real — but it is a love that has already learned to survive loss.
Reading it aloud, you have to find a voice for Ada that is not sentimental — because the passage earns its emotion through precision, not through softness.
And that precision — the way Dickens earns the feeling through craft rather than merely declaring it — brings us back to where we began: the architecture of the novel itself.

The handkerchief travels, the legal language devours, Ada's hair becomes light, and all of it is held inside this extraordinary double narrative — a structure built to show how everything connects, and how connection can be fatal.
Eleanor, Oliver, Caroline — thank you.
We'll continue our exploration of Bleak House after the break — looking at the novel's great set pieces and what Dickens does when he chooses to show rather than to narrate.

segments.title: Laughter in the Abyss: Comedy and Character in Bleak House

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great novel apart to see how it works — and why it still matters.
I'm your host, and today we're exploring one of the novel's most remarkable achievements: its comedy.
Bleak House is a novel about suffering, injustice, and the grinding cruelty of institutions — and it is also, page for page, one of the funniest books in English literature.
To explore how Dickens holds those registers together, I'm joined by three wonderful guests.
Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who brings a craftsperson's eye to the architecture of Dickens's prose.
Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more classic novel audiobooks than anyone alive, and he hears this novel the way a conductor hears a score.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has re-read Bleak House many times and brings the perspective of a deeply devoted, deeply opinionated reader.
Let's begin with the question of what kind of comedy this actually is — because it's not gentle, is it?
No, it is absolutely not gentle — and I think that's the first thing to establish.
Dickens is a satirist with a scalpel, not a tickling feather.
Take the portrait of Lady Dedlock in the early chapters — the omniscient narrator absolutely dismantles her self-image.
She believes herself, as the narrator puts it, to be an inscrutable Being, quite out of the reach and ken of ordinary mortals.
And then the narrator immediately and mercilessly tells us what's actually going on.
"Yet every dim little star revolving about her, from her maid to the manager of the Italian Opera, knows her weaknesses, prejudices, follies, haughtinesses, and caprices."
Every single person in her orbit — and she thinks she's imperious, impenetrable — has her completely figured out.
That's not a comic observation. That's a devastating one wearing a comic mask.
And what's so brilliant structurally is the way the narrator extends that joke into a kind of commercial catalogue.
We get Blaze and Sparkle the jewellers, Sheen and Gloss the mercers, Mr. Sladdery the librarian — each with their own perfectly pitched sales patter.
Those names alone are doing enormous work — they're satirical labels before a word is spoken.
But then the narrator reaches for this extraordinary simile to cap it all.
"who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput"
The Gulliver reference is perfectly chosen — the fashionable class as tiny, self-important ships being towed behind a giant.
The comedy is inseparable from the contempt.
What strikes me every time I re-read that passage is the word majestic.
"The majestic Lilliput" — it's a tiny, perfect joke inside the larger joke.
Lilliput is, by definition, not majestic. And yet Lady Dedlock's world insists on its own grandeur.
That's Dickens in miniature — the language enacts the self-delusion it's describing.
Let's shift to a very different kind of comedy — the comic characters who feel almost too large for the pages that contain them.
Oliver, you have a particular passion for Boythorn, I know.
Boythorn is one of the great pleasures of this novel — full stop.
He's enormous, he's loud, he commits to every syllable of every opinion with his entire body.
And his feud with Sir Leicester Dedlock over a right of way is Dickens at his most joyously absurd.
When Boythorn tells the story, you have to hear the escalation — the fire engine, the chopped-down gate, the peas fired at legs.
"He brings actions for trespass; I bring actions for trespass. He brings actions for assault and battery; I defend them and continue to assault and batter. Ha, ha, ha!"
That "Ha, ha, ha" on the page — three syllables, pure triumph — I've performed it a dozen times and it never gets old.
But what makes it more than a comic set piece is what that feud is about: property, law, class, the suffocating arrogance of the aristocracy.
And the novel makes that satirical point even sharper by placing Boythorn directly against Sir Leicester — who is, by contrast, entirely without self-awareness.
There's that passage in Chapter Sixteen where Sir Leicester reclines amid his ancestral portraits.
The portraits speak to him — or the narrator imagines them speaking — and what they say is unexpectedly beautiful.
"Each of us was a passing reality here and left this coloured shadow of himself and melted into remembrance as dreamy as the distant voices of the rooks now lulling you to rest."
The satirical comedy and the genuine elegy are folded into the same moment — and what the portraits say to Sir Leicester, he entirely misunderstands.
He hears confirmation of his greatness. The narrator hears the rumble of time disposing of him.
I want to come back to something earthier, because the Pardiggle children are utter perfection and I can't let them pass.
Esther watches Mrs. Pardiggle's sons being forced to donate their pocket money to various causes — and the description of their faces is one of the funniest things in the book.
Listen to how Esther puts it.
"We had never seen such dissatisfied children. It was not merely that they were weazened and shrivelled—though they were certainly that too—but they looked absolutely ferocious with discontent."
Ferocious. Not sulky. Not unhappy. Ferocious.
And Esther, who is always so careful and kind, is barely suppressing her laughter as she narrates this.
The comedy is pointed at Mrs. Pardiggle's performative philanthropy — but it comes through the suffering of actual children. It's never quite comfortable.
That's it exactly — never quite comfortable. That's the key to the whole mode.
And then you get Skimpole — who I find funnier and more monstrous on every re-reading.
When Bucket pays Skimpole to betray Jo — and Skimpole constructs this elaborate philosophical argument for why he had no choice but to accept the money —
"Should the Skimpole have refused the note? WHY should the Skimpole have refused the note?"
The third person — the Skimpole — that's the tell. He has abstracted himself entirely from moral accountability.
It's hilarious on the surface and absolutely sickening underneath. A child has been handed to a detective. A child dies.
Dickens doesn't soften either register — he makes you laugh and then makes you feel the laugh curdle.
The third-person self-reference is doing everything there, structurally.
Skimpole has turned himself into a concept — an aesthetic proposition — and that manoeuvre is precisely what makes him dangerous.
What's so brilliant is that the cumulative structure of the speech mimics nursery-rhyme repetition — the house that Jack built.
Skimpole even names it: "like the house that Jack built." He's aware of the absurdity — and weaponises it.
The comedy is the alibi. That's the most chilling thing Dickens does in this novel, I think.
I want to set that against something much lighter — because Jarndyce's eccentricity is comedy of a completely different kind.
There's this small, perfect moment where Ada remembers her mother trying to thank Jarndyce for some generosity.
He spotted her coming through a window.
"he happened to see her through a window coming to the door, and immediately escaped by the back gate, and was not heard of for three months"
Three months. He absconded for three months to avoid a thank-you.
It's pure comedy — but it also tells you everything about the warmth of the man, and his genuine embarrassment at being seen to do good.
In a novel full of people who perform goodness — Mrs. Pardiggle, Skimpole — Jarndyce flees from the very appearance of it.
That's the moral compass of the comedy, isn't it — Jarndyce is the one who earns the warmth precisely because he can't bear it.
And the comedy of that scene is indistinguishable from tenderness.
Dickens can hold all of this at once — the scalpel, the elegy, the warm laugh.
I don't think any other novelist in English has the same range within a single chapter.
The scalpel, the elegy, and the warm laugh — I think that might be the best summary of Bleak House's comedy I've heard.
In our next segment, we'll be turning to the novel's two narrators — Esther and the omniscient voice — and asking how that formal experiment shapes everything we've been discussing today.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Richard's Slow Unraveling: A Life Consumed by Chancery

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, where we spend serious time with one of the greatest novels in the English language.
I'm your host, and today's episode follows one of the novel's most quietly devastating threads: the slow unraveling of Richard Carstone.
Richard begins the novel as a charming, gifted young man with every advantage — except the one that matters most: a settled sense of purpose.
Chancery will do the rest.
With me today are three brilliant readers of this novel, each bringing a different lens to the text.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and teacher of creative writing, fascinated above all by how Dickens constructs his effects — the architecture beneath the story.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and the voice of more classic audiobooks than he'd probably care to count — he comes to every novel as a performer first.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a critic and lifelong rereader of Bleak House, who brings the rare gift of genuine feeling to close reading.
Let's begin with the novel's broader portrait of characters who exist in opposition to Richard — figures whose opacity or rootlessness illuminate what he lacks.
What strikes me when I think about how Dickens builds this arc is that he surrounds Richard with counter-examples — figures who model what rootedness, or its absence, actually looks like.
And the most startling of these, I think, is Tulkinghorn — a man who is all shell and no interior.
Dickens gives us this extraordinary passage describing him standing by a portmanteau while a man lies dead nearby.
"He has shown neither patience nor impatience, nor attention nor abstraction. He has shown nothing but his shell."
And then — the line that follows is one of the great similes in the novel.
"As easily might the tone of a delicate musical instrument be inferred from its case, as the tone of Mr. Tulkinghorn from his case."
That word 'case' — doing double duty as the lawyer's instrument case and as his legal persona — is structurally exact.
Tulkinghorn is pure surface, pure function, no music inside.
Richard, in contrast, has abundant music — he just can't find the instrument.
That simile is astonishing when you read it aloud — the poise of it, the way it pivots on a single word.
As a performer, what I notice is the negative catalogue Dickens builds before it: neither patience nor impatience, neither attention nor abstraction.
It's a kind of via negativa — you learn what Tulkinghorn is by exhausting everything he isn't.
And around him in that scene are three other kinds of human presence — the surgeon's professional detachment, the old man's unction, the woman's awe.
Tulkinghorn is equally removed from all three.
He's the novel's great vacancy — and Richard, in a tragic way, is gradually emptying himself toward the same condition.
There's something else in that chapter that I find almost unbearable — and it's the counterweight to Tulkinghorn's emptiness.
Jo, the crossing-sweeper, is asked what he knows about the dead man, and what he knows is almost nothing.
Except this one thing.
Dickens writes that one cold winter night, the dead man — Nemo — found Jo shivering in a doorway.

"He turned to look at him, and came back, and having questioned him and found that he had not a friend in the world, said, 'Neither have I. Not one!' and gave him the price of a supper and a night's lodging."
Neither have I. Not one.
Two people with nothing — recognizing each other.
That is Dickens at his most morally serious, and it happens in four words.
And notice how that scene radiates outward — Nemo's compassion for Jo is the one human act in a chapter full of official indifference.
The surgeon sees a professional case; Tulkinghorn sees nothing at all; only the dead pauper saw a person.
It's structurally crucial too, because it prepares us to understand what the Chancery world destroys in Richard.
Chancery doesn't just consume money and time — it consumes that capacity for genuine, present-tense attention to another human being.
Which brings us to the scene I think is the hinge of Richard's entire arc — Jarndyce's great speech to him.
It's a wonderful piece of writing because it's simultaneously warm and devastating — Jarndyce loves Richard while telling him exactly what is wrong with him.
Esther records him saying — and this is a speech that rewards being read aloud slowly:
"Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner."
"Constancy in love is a good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy in every kind of effort."
That rhythm — 'means nothing, and is nothing' — is almost biblical.
Jarndyce is performing something here — the formal, loving address of a guardian who can see the disaster coming and is powerless to prevent it.
What makes that speech so painful is that Richard hears it — and agrees with it, in the moment.
He's not a fool and he's not cynical.
He simply cannot maintain constancy — because Chancery has already seeded a competing faith.
And then Esther gives us that image — the two of them, Ada and Richard, walking through the sunlit rooms.

"So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come and making them all years of brightness."
"So they passed away into the shadow and were gone."
It stops you completely.
The sunlight, the shadow, the darkening room — Esther is encoding the whole novel's movement in a single visual gesture.
That passage is formally extraordinary because Esther — the most reticent of narrators about her own foresight — allows herself this moment of prophetic vision.
The sentence moves in three registers: lyric celebration, then the pivot on 'shadow,' then the flat declarative.
'The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over.' — that's the natural world registering what Esther won't say plainly.
It's an old poetic device — the pathetic fallacy — but Dickens earns it because the emotion is already there, fully prepared.
And then, almost immediately, Dickens gives us the clinical diagnosis — Mrs. Badger delivering her verdict on Richard's future in medicine.
Mrs. Badger is one of those magnificent Dickensian figures who is simultaneously comic and devastating.
She says of Richard — and the contrast with young Woodcourt is the knife in it:

"Young men like Mr. Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a very little money and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment."
'Considerable endurance and disappointment' — that's what vocation actually costs. And Richard won't pay it.
What's beautiful about Mrs. Badger is that she's not unkind — she's just a woman who has observed human beings for a long time and knows what she sees.
She also says something that I think is the plainest diagnosis in the novel: that Richard feels medicine is 'a tiresome pursuit.'
Not wrong, not frightening — merely tiresome.
And Dickens — through Mrs. Badger — is showing us that Richard's problem isn't weakness of character in any simple sense.
It's the absence of vocation — and Chancery has offered him a counterfeit substitute.
The case will give his life meaning — or so he believes — and that belief is what destroys him.
That's the extraordinary trap Dickens has set — Chancery presents itself as the organizing principle that Richard lacks.
It mimics vocation. It mimics constancy. It mimics a future.
And Jarndyce, who has watched Chancery for decades, can see it happening — which is why that speech has such urgency.
'If you entertain the supposition that any real success ever was or could be wrested from Fortune by fits and starts, leave that wrong idea here' — it's the most direct warning in the book.
Richard hears it. He agrees with it. He walks out into the sunlight with Ada — and forgets every word.
What strikes me, listening to all of this, is that Dickens builds Richard's destruction not through melodrama but through accumulation — small failures of attention, of commitment, of constancy.
Each of the passages we've looked at today — Tulkinghorn's emptiness, Nemo's compassion, Jarndyce's warning, that ravishing image of the sunlit rooms — they all converge on one question.
What does it cost a person to live without a genuine vocation — and to mistake litigation for one?
We'll carry that question forward as we continue to follow Richard's arc through the novel.
Thank you to Eleanor, Oliver, and Caroline — and to you for listening to Bleak House Unpacked.

segments.title: Secrets and Shadows: Lady Dedlock's Double Life

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great novel seriously — all its comedy, its darkness, its extraordinary architecture.
I'm joined today by three wonderful guides through the novel.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative-writing teacher who cares above all about how Dickens builds his effects — the craft beneath the surface.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels on audio than almost anyone alive — he comes to the text as a performer, hearing every rhythm and every pause.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and lifelong reader of Bleak House, someone who has re-read it many times and still finds new things to love and argue about.
Today's segment is about secrets — and about the extraordinary figure at the centre of this novel's hidden world: Lady Dedlock.
Eleanor, let's begin with you — because I think the architecture question is already fascinating here.
What strikes me immediately about these early chapters is how Dickens uses documents — letters, affidavits, handwriting — as the connective tissue of the plot.
Sir Leicester reading Tulkinghorn's letter aloud is such a deft piece of staging.
He fumbles with his eyeglass, misfinds the right passage, reads the wrong line first — and all of this delay is exquisite torment for Lady Dedlock, and for us.
And then finally Tulkinghorn's words arrive, and they are almost unbearably precise.
"I have something to tell her on her return in reference to the person who copied the affidavit in the Chancery suit, which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity. I have seen him."
Three words at the end. 'I have seen him.' The whole weight of exposure carried in a single short sentence.
Dickens knows exactly when to compress — and that compression is where the menace lives.
And what makes it even more theatrical is that Tulkinghorn isn't even in the room — he's present only through his letter, read aloud by an oblivious husband.
He has arranged things so that his message arrives in the most exposed possible way.
And then he appears in person — and Dickens gives us one of the great character descriptions in the novel.
"He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress."
Every limb. Every crease. You can hear the relish in that repetition.
And then comes the line that I think defines him completely.
"He is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself."
That's the terror of Tulkinghorn in a single clause — utterly self-contained, utterly without weakness.
What I keep coming back to is the mutual watching — the scene where they face each other and neither gives anything away.
Dickens is so precise about it — Sir Leicester just stares at the fire, blissfully unaware, while these two conduct a silent war in his presence.
And the narrator articulates the unseen interior drama with this extraordinary passage.
"Whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares."
That word 'evermore' — repeated three times — gives it this gothic, almost incantatory quality.
It isn't just a scene between two people. It's a condition — a permanent state of mutual siege.
That observation about the gothic register is exactly right — and it connects to something larger about how Dickens constructs Lady Dedlock's secret.
He parcels the information out with extraordinary care — and a lot of it comes to us through intermediaries, through legal language, through reported speech.
Even the revelation of the connection to Esther is filtered through Jarndyce, who is himself quoting from memory a message received through Kenge.
And the woman — Lady Dedlock — stipulates one thing above all.
"That more than this she would never — and he was well persuaded of the steadfastness of her resolution — for any human consideration disclose."
'For any human consideration.' That phrase is doing enormous work.
She has placed her secret beyond the reach of love, money, argument — everything human. That's an extraordinary, and rather terrifying, act of will.
And yet — and this is what makes her such a compelling character — there are cracks in that composure.
The very fact that she enquired about the handwriting — that she let her curiosity show, however briefly, to Tulkinghorn — that's the slip that sets everything in motion.
A woman who could truly suppress herself would never have asked the question. Part of her wanted to be found.
Or perhaps she simply could not help it — because the connection to the past is not just a secret. It's grief.
That word 'grief' — yes. And I think the passage with the dying infant makes that grief almost unbearably physical.
We're in a completely different register there — Esther and Ada visiting a desperately poor family — and the death is rendered with absolute, terrible brevity.
Ada bends to touch the baby's face — this instinctive, tender gesture — and Esther pulls her back.
"As she did so, I saw what happened and drew her back. The child died."
Three words. 'The child died.' I find that almost unbearable every time.
No sentiment added — no adjectives — just the fact, placed like a stone.
That economy is Esther's narrative voice at its most powerful — and I don't think it's accidental that Dickens reserves it for moments of death.
Esther tends to qualify, to soften, to apologise for her own feelings — but here she doesn't.
She simply acts — she draws Ada back — and then she reports the fact.
It's as if at the moment of true extremity, the prose strips itself bare.
And that poverty of ornament — in the midst of a novel famous for its excess — is devastating.
That contrast — the stripped-bare and the baroque, Esther's plain grief and Tulkinghorn's sinister grandeur — feels like it's at the heart of what this novel is doing.
Secrets in Bleak House aren't just plot machinery — they are a way of showing how completely one life can be hidden inside another.
Eleanor, Oliver, Caroline — thank you. We'll return to Lady Dedlock's world, and to the question of what it costs to maintain it, a little later in this episode.

segments.title: The Crossing-Sweep's Testament: Jo and the Cost of Society's Indifference

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great novel apart — chapter by chapter, image by image — to understand why it still feels so urgent today.
I'm your host, and today we're turning to one of the most quietly devastating sequences in all of Dickens — the testimony and inner life of Jo, the crossing-sweeper.
Jo is perhaps the most stripped-down human being in Victorian fiction — no surname, no schooling, barely a self in the eyes of the law.
To help us think through what Dickens is doing here, I'm joined by three wonderful guests.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose eye for the architecture of prose is, quite simply, unmatched.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels than anyone alive, and he reads Dickens the way Dickens wanted — as a performer alive to every rhythm and comic turn.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first encountered this novel as a teenager and has never quite let it go — she brings a reader's fierce emotional loyalty to everything she discusses.
Let's begin with Jo's testimony at the inquest — which is, on its surface, a comic scene, but I think something much darker is happening underneath it.
What Dickens does in that inquest scene is structurally audacious, and I think it's worth slowing down to feel the full force of it.
He gives us Mrs. Piper first — that wonderful, unstoppable, parenthetical witness — and she is genuinely funny.
The comedy is doing serious work, though — it shows a community that has assembled a complete portrait of a man from rumour and fear.
Dickens tells us she has, quote, a good deal to say — and then the whole torrential parenthetical flood arrives.
"Why, Mrs. Piper has a good deal to say, chiefly in parentheses and without punctuation, but not much to tell."
That contrast — much to say, not much to tell — is the whole critique of the inquest in a single clause.
And then Jo arrives, and the comedy stops dead.
I want to go straight to that testimony, because when you read it aloud, the effect is almost unbearable.
Dickens sets Jo's words down as a kind of staccato list — each fact smaller and more terrible than the last.
Here it is, exactly as Dickens wrote it:
"No father, no mother, no friends. Never been to school."
Four negatives in eight words — and then the simplest possible conclusion: never been to school.
As a performer, the temptation is to milk those lines — but Dickens's genius is that they need no milking.
The nakedness of the syntax is the feeling. You just have to get out of the way and let it land.
What strikes me — rereading it again for today — is the line about the broom and the lie.
Jo can't read, can't spell his own name, doesn't know what happens after death.
But Dickens gives him two pieces of moral knowledge — that a broom is a broom, and that it's wicked to lie.
And then comes this extraordinary line:
"Don't recollect who told him about the broom or about the lie, but knows both."
He knows what is right without being able to say where that knowledge came from. That is a kind of grace.
And the institution — the inquest — is about to throw him out anyway, because he can't swear a proper oath.
Caroline, that word — grace — is exactly the word Dickens reaches for himself.
Because after the inquest dismisses Jo, Dickens turns directly to address him — the narrator steps out of the story and speaks to the character.
It is one of the most formally unusual moves in the novel.
He writes — and I want to read this carefully:
"Jo, is it thou? Well, well! Though a rejected witness, who can't exactly say what will be done to him in greater hands than men's, thou art not quite in outer darkness."
That archaic second person — 'thou,' 'thy,' 'art' — is Dickens reaching for something like scripture.
When the law's language fails Jo, Dickens finds a different register entirely.
And then Dickens lands the payload of the whole passage — Jo's own words, rendered in that brilliant phonetic dialect.
The narrator says there is — and I'm going to read this because the phrasing matters enormously:
"There is something like a distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: 'He wos wery good to me, he wos!'"
'Something like a distant ray' — not redemption, not salvation, not even comfort. Something like.
Dickens is being scrupulously, heartbreakingly honest about how little the universe is offering this child.
And yet — he wos wery good to me. That is Jo's entire theology. His entire world.
I think about Jo alongside the great pleading scenes later in the novel — Mrs. Rouncewell before Lady Dedlock, for instance.
Because there too you have someone who is, by the world's reckoning, voiceless — a servant — having to beg for elementary justice.
Mrs. Rouncewell's speech is extraordinary for its self-awareness about her own social position.
She says to Lady Dedlock — and this is devastating:

"My Lady, you may have some proud or angry reasons for disdaining to utter something that you know; if so, pray, oh, pray, think of a faithful servant whose whole life has been passed in this family which she dearly loves."
She acknowledges Lady Dedlock's right to withhold — and then begs her to overcome it anyway.
Jo cannot do that. He doesn't have the words, the position, the access.
What Jo has is that one fact: he wos wery good to me.
The connection Caroline's drawing is exactly right, and I'd add that Dickens sets these figures against the system's own language.
Think of Jarndyce in Chapter 62, when he refuses even to look at the newly discovered will.
He says — and this is a man who has watched Chancery devour lives for decades:
"The plain truth is, I have forsworn and abjured the whole business these many years, and my soul is sick of it."
'My soul is sick of it' — that is the emotional inverse of Jo's grace.
Jo is innocent and excluded. Jarndyce is knowing and exhausted.
Both are defined by what the law has done — or refused to do — for them.
What I keep returning to is the comedy Dickens smuggles into the darkness — Mrs. Piper and her magnificent parentheses.
She describes the dead man's supposedly ferocious manner — spelled, in her testimony, 'feariocious.'
And she worries, on the record, about her son Johnny — who, she says, the deceased would have attacked with a pickaxe from his pocket.
But she adds — and this is the Dickensian comic sting — that she never actually saw a pickaxe, or any weapon — quote, 'far from it.'
"Never however see the plaintive take a pick-axe or any other wepping far from it."
'Far from it' — she's exonerating the man she just spent three hundred words condemning.
The comedy is the tragedy. This is the evidence on which a dead man's character is assessed.
I think that's the heart of it — Dickens shows us the machinery that produces indifference, and he makes it funny so we can barely stand how sad it is.
Jo has no name that anyone cares to record, no family, no education — and his only testimony to the value of a human life is a misspelled sentence in dialect.
And Dickens insists that sentence is worth more than everything the court has to say.
In our next segment, we'll move to another kind of exclusion — the women Bleak House places at its centre, and what the novel asks of them and does to them.

segments.title: Closing: Redemption and Ruin—What Dickens Leaves Us With

utterances.text: We've spent this episode tracing the architecture of Bleak House — its satire, its sorrow, its extraordinary range.
For our closing segment, I want to ask each of you what Dickens finally leaves us with — what lingers.
Is it redemption, ruin, or something more complicated than either?
Eleanor, you've been looking at the novel's institutional satire — let's start with you.
What strikes me, coming to the end, is how the novel separates the institutional from the personal — and then shows us that separation is itself a kind of tragedy.
The law doesn't change. Chancery grinds on.
Dickens gives us that magnificent piece of parliamentary satire — the Vholes defence — which is essentially a machine for defeating reform through respectability.
The passage builds to this devastating mock-parliamentary exchange, where every question that could lead to change is strangled by one answer.
"Mr. Vholes is considered, in the profession, a MOST respectable man."
And Dickens tells us that single answer proved fatal to the inquiry — for ten years.
That is the comic form of institutional evil — not malice but inertia wrapped in propriety.
The ruin is systemic. And Dickens knows it will outlast his novel.
Eleanor's absolutely right that the institution doesn't yield — and what makes it so brilliant is that Dickens gives you the comedy and the horror at once.
Kenge's speech is genuinely funny — the cadences are those of a man who has rehearsed this so many times he no longer hears how absurd it is.
Listen to the rhythm of it — the escalating questions — delay, expense, unspeakable vexation — and then the attorney's breezy reply.
"They have never given ME any vexation; quite the contrary."
That 'ME' is doing so much work — the emphasis belongs entirely on himself, the system's willing servant.
But then I come to the personal stories — Richard and Ada — and the comedy drains away entirely.
Because Richard is destroyed not by wickedness but by hope — misplaced, consuming, Chancery-fed hope.
What breaks my heart is how Dickens shows you the tenderness before the ruin — so that you understand exactly what is being lost.
There's that early chapter where Richard and Ada have just confided in Esther — they sit one on each side of her, like children placing themselves in safe hands.
And Esther gives us this sentence that is, to me, one of the most quietly devastating in the whole novel.
"They went on in their own wild way for a little while — I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself."
'I enjoyed it too much myself.' That small admission from Esther is everything — she knows what they don't yet know, that this is precious.
And then she steers them gently toward what enduring love requires — constancy, fortitude, perseverance, each always for the other's sake.
Those words carry such weight because we know — as readers, on a second reading especially — how much Richard will fail them.
That structural irony is exactly what I mean about Dickens's craft — he's always writing to be re-read.
And then there's Mr. Jarndyce's speech to the young couple — which is its own small masterpiece of tone.
He acknowledges he had imagined their union — but with that repeated insistence: 'afar off, Rick, afar off.'
"But that was afar off, Rick, afar off!"
That repetition is doing so much emotional work — it's tenderness, it's a gentle warning, it's the older man putting distance between hope and demand.
Dickens writes Jarndyce at his most generous here — and it makes what follows all the more painful.
When I've read Jarndyce aloud, that speech is one I always slow down for — because there's real music in how the generosity and the warning are braided together.
He goes on to say — and this is extraordinary — that he will assume their love endures, but if it doesn't, they must not be ashamed to tell him.

"If you DO change — if you DO come to find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and woman than you were as boy and girl — don't be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be nothing monstrous or uncommon in it."
'Nothing monstrous or uncommon' — that phrase alone tells you the whole character.
He is the one adult in the novel who refuses to deal in illusions — and yet does it without extinguishing hope.
And yet — because this is Bleak House — we know it won't be enough.
The chain of flowers Jarndyce mentions — his own image — does become a chain of lead.
Not because their love isn't real, but because the law gets into Richard — and it corrodes everything it touches.
That's what I find so unsparing about this novel.
Good people, loving clearly, counselled wisely — and still, ruin finds its way in.
That image — the chain of flowers becoming a chain of lead — seems to me to hold the entire novel's argument in miniature.
Dickens does not promise us that virtue protects you.
He only promises that the record of tenderness — Esther's voice, Jarndyce's steadiness — survives.
Eleanor, Oliver, Caroline — it has been a genuine pleasure to think through this novel with you.
Bleak House rewards every return — and this conversation has reminded me why.
For our listeners: thank you for joining us on Bleak House Unpacked.
We'll be back with more of the best in classic fiction — read closely, talked about honestly, and enjoyed without apology.

c7:p59.text:
“She had been a lady of a handsome figure and a noble carriage. She
never complained of the change; she never spoke to any one of being
crippled or of being in pain, but day by day she tried to walk upon
the terrace, and with the help of the stone balustrade, went up and
down, up and down, up and down, in sun and shadow, with greater
difficulty every day. At last, one afternoon her husband (to whom she
had never, on any persuasion, opened her lips since that night),
standing at the great south window, saw her drop upon the pavement.
He hastened down to raise her, but she repulsed him as he bent over
her, and looking at him fixedly and coldly, said, ‘I will die here
where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I
will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when
calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen
for my step!’”
c7:p59.summary: The crippled lady, after her husband finds her on the pavement, looks at him coldly and curses the Dedlock family: she will walk the terrace forever as a warning of coming calamity and disgrace.
c7:p59.best_quote: I will die here where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen for my step!

c36:p18.text:
I was resting at my favourite point after a long ramble, and Charley
was gathering violets at a little distance from me. I had been
looking at the Ghost’s Walk lying in a deep shade of masonry afar off
and picturing to myself the female shape that was said to haunt it
when I became aware of a figure approaching through the wood. The
perspective was so long and so darkened by leaves, and the shadows of
the branches on the ground made it so much more intricate to the eye,
that at first I could not discern what figure it was. By little and
little it revealed itself to be a woman’s—a lady’s—Lady Dedlock’s.
She was alone and coming to where I sat with a much quicker step, I
observed to my surprise, than was usual with her.
c36:p18.summary: As Esther rests at her favorite spot, a woman emerges through the wood—Lady Dedlock, approaching with unusual haste and emotion.

c56:p51.text:
“Now, Mr. Jarndyce”—Mr. Bucket has read his face with the greatest
attention all along—“I speak to you as a gentleman of a humane
heart, and under such pressing circumstances as don’t often happen.
If ever delay was dangerous, it’s dangerous now; and if ever you
couldn’t afterwards forgive yourself for causing it, this is the
time. Eight or ten hours, worth, as I tell you, a hundred pound
apiece at least, have been lost since Lady Dedlock disappeared. I am
charged to find her. I am Inspector Bucket. Besides all the rest
that’s heavy on her, she has upon her, as she believes, suspicion of
murder. If I follow her alone, she, being in ignorance of what Sir
Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, has communicated to me, may be driven to
desperation. But if I follow her in company with a young lady,
answering to the description of a young lady that she has a
tenderness for—I ask no question, and I say no more than that—she
will give me credit for being friendly. Let me come up with her and
be able to have the hold upon her of putting that young lady for’ard,
and I’ll save her and prevail with her if she is alive. Let me come
up with her alone—a hard matter—and I’ll do my best, but I don’t
answer for what the best may be. Time flies; it’s getting on for one
o’clock. When one strikes, there’s another hour gone, and it’s worth
a thousand pound now instead of a hundred.”
c56:p51.summary: Mr. Bucket makes a compelling case to Mr. Jarndyce: without Esther, Lady Dedlock may despair and take her own life; with Esther's presence, Lady Dedlock may trust him and be saved. He emphasizes that time is critical and frames the request as a matter of life and death.
c56:p51.best_quote: If I follow her alone, she, being in ignorance of what Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, has communicated to me, may be driven to desperation. But if I follow her in company with a young lady, answering to the description of a young lady that she has a tenderness for—I ask no question, and I say no more than that—she will give me credit for being friendly.

c8:p117.text:
How little I thought, when I raised my handkerchief to look upon the
tiny sleeper underneath and seemed to see a halo shine around the
child through Ada’s drooping hair as her pity bent her head—how
little I thought in whose unquiet bosom that handkerchief would come
to lie after covering the motionless and peaceful breast! I only
thought that perhaps the Angel of the child might not be all
unconscious of the woman who replaced it with so compassionate a
hand; not all unconscious of her presently, when we had taken leave,
and left her at the door, by turns looking, and listening in terror
for herself, and saying in her old soothing manner, “Jenny, Jenny!”
c8:p117.summary: Esther reflects on the handkerchief covering the baby and wonders about its future journey, expressing her hope that the woman's compassion is recognized by the Angel watching over the child and Jenny.
c8:p117.best_quote: How little I thought, when I raised my handkerchief to look upon the tiny sleeper underneath and seemed to see a halo shine around the child through Ada's drooping hair as her pity bent her head—how little I thought in whose unquiet bosom that handkerchief would come to lie after covering the motionless and peaceful breast!

c23:p37.text:
We walked a little way without speaking, and presently Richard
addressed me in his frankest and most feeling manner, thus: “My dear
Esther, I understand you, and I wish to heaven I were a more constant
sort of fellow. I don’t mean constant to Ada, for I love her
dearly—better and better every day—but constant to myself.
(Somehow, I mean something that I can’t very well express, but you’ll
make it out.) If I were a more constant sort of fellow, I should have
held on either to Badger or to Kenge and Carboy like grim death, and
should have begun to be steady and systematic by this time, and
shouldn’t be in debt,  and—”
c23:p37.summary: Richard makes an earnest and heartfelt confession to Esther that he wishes he were more constant, both to himself and to his various professional pursuits, and admits his financial troubles.
c23:p37.best_quote: I understand you, and I wish to heaven I were a more constant sort of fellow...If I were a more constant sort of fellow, I should have held on either to Badger or to Kenge and Carboy like grim death, and should have begun to be steady and systematic by this time, and shouldn't be in debt, and—

c60:p94.text:
“Pardon me,” returned Mr. Vholes, going on in exactly the same inward
and dispassionate manner. “Mr. C. takes certain interests under
certain wills disputed in the suit. It is a term we use. In reference
to Mr. C,’s pursuit of his interests, I mentioned to you, Miss
Summerson, the first time I had the pleasure of seeing you, in my
desire that everything should be openly carried on—I used those
words, for I happened afterwards to note them in my diary, which is
producible at any time—I mentioned to you that Mr. C. had laid down
the principle of watching his own interests, and that when a client
of mine laid down a principle which was not of an immoral (that is to
say, unlawful) nature, it devolved upon me to carry it out. I HAVE
carried it out; I do carry it out. But I will not smooth things over
to any connexion of Mr. C.’s on any account. As open as I was to Mr.
Jarndyce, I am to you. I regard it in the light of a professional
duty to be so, though it can be charged to no one. I openly say,
unpalatable as it may be, that I consider Mr. C.’s affairs in a very
bad way, that I consider Mr. C. himself in a very bad way, and that I
regard this as an exceedingly ill-advised marriage. Am I here, sir?
Yes, I thank you; I am here, Mr. C., and enjoying the pleasure of
some agreeable conversation with Miss Summerson, for which I have to
thank you very much, sir!”
c60:p94.summary: Vholes meticulously documents his conversation in his diary and explains that he must openly declare his belief that Richard's affairs are in very bad way and the marriage was ill-advised, all as professional duty; he then abruptly switches to greeting Richard's arrival.
c60:p94.best_quote: I HAVE carried it out; I do carry it out. But I will not smooth things over to any connexion of Mr. C.'s on any account. As open as I was to Mr. Jarndyce, I am to you. I regard it in the light of a professional duty to be so, though it can be charged to no one.

c41:p65.text:
“Therefore,” says Mr. Tulkinghorn, pursuing his case in his jog-trot
style, “I have much to consider. This is to be hushed up if it can
be. How can it be, if Sir Leicester is driven out of his wits or laid
upon a death-bed? If I inflicted this shock upon him to-morrow
morning, how could the immediate change in him be accounted for? What
could have caused it? What could have divided you? Lady Dedlock, the
wall-chalking and the street-crying would come on directly, and you
are to remember that it would not affect you merely (whom I cannot at
all consider in this business) but your husband, Lady Dedlock, your
husband.”
c41:p65.summary: Tulkinghorn argues that any sudden change in Sir Leicester's state would raise questions and lead to scandal; he must consider how to manage the shock without destroying Sir Leicester.
c41:p65.best_quote: If I inflicted this shock upon him to-morrow morning, how could the immediate change in him be accounted for? What could have caused it?

c51:p64.text:
He was leaning on his arm saying these words in a meditative voice
and looking at the ground when my darling rose, put off her bonnet,
kneeled down beside him with her golden hair falling like sunlight on
his head, clasped her two arms round his neck, and turned her face to
me. Oh, what a loving and devoted face I saw!
c51:p64.summary: Ada rises and kneels beside Richard with her golden hair cascading over him, embracing him devotedly and turning her face toward Esther.

c60:p123.text:
“If that little creature should fail too, Esther, I still look
forward. I look forward a long while, through years and years, and
think that then, when I am growing old, or when I am dead perhaps, a
beautiful woman, his daughter, happily married, may be proud of him
and a blessing to him. Or that a generous brave man, as handsome as
he used to be, as hopeful, and far more happy, may walk in the
sunshine with him, honouring his grey head and saying to himself, ‘I
thank God this is my father! Ruined by a fatal inheritance, and
restored through me!’”
c60:p123.summary: Ada envisions a future where her child—whether daughter or son—might redeem Richard through love and pride, providing meaning to his ruin through restoration in the next generation.
c60:p123.best_quote: Or that a generous brave man, as handsome as he used to be, as hopeful, and far more happy, may walk in the sunshine with him, honouring his grey head and saying to himself, 'I thank God this is my father! Ruined by a fatal inheritance, and restored through me!'

c2:p12.text:
Has Mr. Tulkinghorn any idea of this himself? It may be so, or it may
not, but there is this remarkable circumstance to be noted in
everything associated with my Lady Dedlock as one of a class—as one
of the leaders and representatives of her little world. She supposes
herself to be an inscrutable Being, quite out of the reach and ken of
ordinary mortals—seeing herself in her glass, where indeed she looks
so. Yet every dim little star revolving about her, from her maid to
the manager of the Italian Opera, knows her weaknesses, prejudices,
follies, haughtinesses, and caprices and lives upon as accurate a
calculation and as nice a measure of her moral nature as her
dressmaker takes of her physical proportions. Is a new dress, a new
custom, a new singer, a new dancer, a new form of jewellery, a new
dwarf or giant, a new chapel, a new anything, to be set up? There are
deferential people in a dozen callings whom my Lady Dedlock suspects
of nothing but prostration before her, who can tell you how to manage
her as if she were a baby, who do nothing but nurse her all their
lives, who, humbly affecting to follow with profound subservience,

most stiff-necked, arrogant imbecile, pig-headed numskull, ever, by

a walking-stick’s! The whole of that family are the most solemnly
conceited and consummate blockheads! But it’s no matter; he should
not shut up my path if he were fifty baronets melted into one and
living in a hundred Chesney Wolds, one within another, like the ivory
balls in a Chinese carving. The fellow, by his agent, or secretary,
or somebody, writes to me ‘Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, presents
his compliments to Mr. Lawrence Boythorn, and has to call his
attention to the fact that the green pathway by the old
parsonage-house, now the property of Mr. Lawrence Boythorn, is Sir
Leicester’s right of way, being in fact a portion of the park of
Chesney Wold, and that Sir Leicester finds it convenient to close up
the same.’ I write to the fellow, ‘Mr. Lawrence Boythorn presents his
compliments to Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, and has to call HIS
attention to the fact that he totally denies the whole of Sir
Leicester Dedlock’s positions on every possible subject and has to
add, in reference to closing up the pathway, that he will be glad to
see the man who may undertake to do it.’ The fellow sends a most
abandoned villain with one eye to construct a gateway. I play upon
that execrable scoundrel with a fire-engine until the breath is
nearly driven out of his body. The fellow erects a gate in the night.
I chop it down and burn it in the morning. He sends his myrmidons to
come over the fence and pass and repass. I catch them in humane man
traps, fire split peas at their legs, play upon them with the
engine—resolve to free mankind from the insupportable burden of the

I bring actions for trespass. He brings actions for assault and
battery; I defend them and continue to assault and batter. Ha, ha,
ha!”

There he was, of course. They brought a chair on either side of me,
and put me between them, and really seemed to have fallen in love
with me instead of one another, they were so confiding, and so
trustful, and so fond of me. They went on in their own wild way for a
little while—I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself—and
then we gradually fell to considering how young they were, and how
there must be a lapse of several years before this early love could
come to anything, and how it could come to happiness only if it were
real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do
their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and
perseverance, each always for the other’s sake. Well! Richard said
that he would work his fingers to the bone for Ada, and Ada said that
she would work her fingers to the bone for Richard, and they called
me all sorts of endearing and sensible names, and we sat there,
advising and talking, half the night. Finally, before we parted, I
gave them my promise to speak to their cousin John to-morrow.

c13:p113.text:
“Rick,” said Mr. Jarndyce, “I am glad to have won your confidence. I
hope to preserve it. When I contemplated these relations between us
four which have so brightened my life and so invested it with new
interests and pleasures, I certainly did contemplate, afar off, the
possibility of you and your pretty cousin here (don’t be shy, Ada,
don’t be shy, my dear!) being in a mind to go through life together.
I saw, and do see, many reasons to make it desirable. But that was
afar off, Rick, afar off!”
c13:p113.summary: Mr. Jarndyce addresses Richard and Ada, confirming he is glad to have their confidence and that he did contemplate their union as a possibility.

c13:p115.text:
“Well!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “That’s rational. Now, hear me, my dears!
I might tell you that you don’t know your own minds yet, that a
thousand things may happen to divert you from one another, that it is
well this chain of flowers you have taken up is very easily broken,
or it might become a chain of lead. But I will not do that. Such
wisdom will come soon enough, I dare say, if it is to come at all. I
will assume that a few years hence you will be in your hearts to one
another what you are to-day. All I say before speaking to you
according to that assumption is, if you DO change—if you DO come to
find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and
woman than you were as boy and girl (your manhood will excuse me,
Rick!)—don’t be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be
nothing monstrous or uncommon in it. I am only your friend and
distant kinsman. I have no power over you whatever. But I wish and
hope to retain your confidence if I do nothing to forfeit it.”
c13:p115.summary: Mr. Jarndyce counsels Ada and Richard that while he assumes their love will endure, if they change he will remain their confidant and will not judge them.
